lead: A member carries load, and its section resists that load with internal force resultants. Three resultants matter first: axial force P, bending moment M and torque T. Each makes a simple stress pattern: uniform normal stress from P, linear normal stress from M, and shear stress that grows with radius from T. The formulas σ = P/A, σ = My/I and τ = Tr/J let you size a shaft, bracket or bolt before any detail design. They are used wherever a quick strength check is needed, from a pump shaft to a fan hub.
prereq: You need: load types from 1.5, and area and second moment of area from basic mechanics.

sections.h3: Direct stress: force spread over area

blocks.text: An axial force P acts along the centroidal axis of a section. P is in newtons (N). Area A is the cross-section area in square metres (m²). Direct stress is σ = P/A. σ is normal stress in pascals (Pa); 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa. The stress is uniform over the section when the load is axial and the section is far from the load application point. Near a hole, keyway or load point the stress is not uniform; that is stress concentration, covered in Unit 2. Tension is positive, compression negative by convention. A 30 kN compressive load on a 1.2566×10⁻³ m² area gives 23.87 MPa compression. Use the net area for a threaded rod or a plate with a hole. Direct shear uses the same form, τ = V/A, where V is shear force; the area is the one that resists sliding.

blocks.where: σ is direct normal stress in Pa; P is axial force in N; A is cross-section area in m².

sections.h3: Bending stress: moment bends the section

blocks.text: Bending moment M is in newton metres (N·m). It makes normal stress that changes linearly across the depth. The neutral axis is the line where bending stress is zero; for a symmetric section under pure bending it passes through the centroid. Let y be distance from the neutral axis in metres (m). Second moment of area I is I = ∫ y² dA, in m⁴. For a solid circle of diameter d, I = πd⁴/64. Bending stress is σ = M y / I. σ is normal stress in Pa; it is positive on one side and negative on the other. The maximum is at the farthest fibre, y = c. Then σmax = M c / I = M / Z, where section modulus Z = I/c in m³. For a solid circle, Z = πd³/32. Assumptions: linear elastic material, small deflection, plane sections remain plane. These hold for slender beams away from loads and supports. For a curved beam the neutral axis shifts; see 1.9. For a shaft, bending stress is normal stress along the shaft axis.
σ = M y / I    and    σ<sub>max</sub> = M c / I = M / Z
blocks.where: σ is bending normal stress in Pa; M is bending moment in N·m; y is distance from the neutral axis in m; I is second moment of area in m⁴; c is distance to the farthest fibre in m; Z = I/c is section modulus in m³.

sections.h3: Torsion: torque twists a circular shaft

blocks.text: Torque T is a moment about the shaft axis, in N·m. In a circular shaft, torsion gives shear stress τ that is zero on the axis and maximum at the surface. Let r be radial distance from the axis in m; at the surface r = d/2. Polar second moment of area J = ∫ ρ² dA, in m⁴, where ρ is the radial coordinate. For a solid circle, J = πd⁴/32. Torsional shear stress is τ = T r / J. τ is in Pa. The maximum is at r = d/2: τmax = T (d/2) / J = T / Zp, where polar modulus Zp = J/(d/2) in m³. For a solid circle, Zp = πd³/16. Assumptions: circular section, linear elastic, small twist, plane sections remain plane and rotate as rigid discs. Hollow shafts use J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32, with D outside and d inside. Torsion stress is shear, not normal. Do not add it directly to bending normal stress; combine them through principal stress, see 1.7. Shaft design with bending and torsion together is in Unit 3.
τ = T r / J    and    τ<sub>max</sub> = T (d/2) / J = T / Z<sub>p</sub>
blocks.where: τ is torsional shear stress in Pa; T is torque in N·m; r is radial distance from the axis in m; J is polar second moment of area in m⁴; d is shaft diameter in m; Z<sub>p</sub> = J/(d/2) is polar modulus in m³.

figure.caption: A single resultant splits into axial force, bending moment and torque. Notice that only torsion gives shear stress; the other two give normal stress.

spec.aria: The three internal resultants produce a uniform axial stress, a linear bending stress and a torsional shear stress that grows with radius.

examples.question: A 40 mm diameter solid shaft carries an axial compressive load of 30 kN, a bending moment of 600 N·m and a torque of 450 N·m. Calculate the direct stress, the maximum bending stress and the maximum torsional shear stress at the surface.
steps: Direct stress magnitude: σ<sub>d</sub> = P/A = 30,000 / 1.2566×10⁻³ = 23.87×10⁶ Pa = 23.87 MPa. The load is compressive, so the sign is negative.
Second moment of area: I = πd⁴/64 = π(0.040)⁴/64 = 1.2566×10⁻⁷ m⁴.
Distance to surface: y = d/2 = 0.020 m. Maximum bending stress: σ<sub>b</sub> = M y / I = 600 × 0.020 / 1.2566×10⁻⁷ = 95.49×10⁶ Pa = 95.49 MPa. Equivalently Z = 6.283×10⁻⁶ m³ and σ<sub>b</sub> = M/Z.
Polar second moment: J = πd⁴/32 = 2.5133×10⁻⁷ m⁴. Radius: r = d/2 = 0.020 m.
Maximum torsional shear stress: τ = T r / J = 450 × 0.020 / 2.5133×10⁻⁷ = 35.81×10⁶ Pa = 35.81 MPa. Equivalently Z<sub>p</sub> = 1.2566×10⁻⁵ m³ and τ = T/Z<sub>p</sub>.
examples.answer: At the surface, the direct stress is 23.87 MPa compressive, the maximum bending stress is 95.49 MPa, and the maximum torsional shear stress is 35.81 MPa.
examples.check:
import math
d = 0.040
P = 30000.0
M = 600.0
T = 450.0
A = math.pi * d**2 / 4
sigma_d = P / A / 1e6
I = math.pi * d**4 / 64
y = d / 2
sigma_b = M * y / I / 1e6
J = math.pi * d**4 / 32
r = d / 2
tau = T * r / J / 1e6
print(round(sigma_d, 2))
print(round(sigma_b, 2))
print(round(tau, 2))

traps: Using diameter instead of radius in τ = Tr/J, or using d instead of d/2 as the distance to the surface in bending.
Adding bending normal stress and torsional shear stress as if they were the same type; combine them through principal stress.
Using I for torsion or J for bending; for a solid circle J = 2I.
Using the gross area for direct stress at a threaded rod or a plate with a hole; use the net area.
Mixing units: M and T in N·m with y or r in mm gives stress in N/mm² = MPa only after correct conversion.

quiz.q: State the direct stress formula and define each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: σ = P/A. σ is normal stress in Pa; P is axial force in N; A is cross-section area in m².

quiz.q: Why is bending stress zero at the neutral axis?
quiz.a: At the neutral axis y = 0 in σ = My/I, so the linear bending stress distribution gives zero stress there. The material at that line neither stretches nor compresses in pure bending.

quiz.q: A solid shaft of diameter 50 mm carries a bending moment of 800 N·m. Find the maximum bending stress.
A 30 mm diameter solid shaft carries a torque of 300 N·m. Find the maximum torsional shear stress.
For the same solid shaft diameter and equal numerical values of bending moment and torque, which maximum stress is larger and by what ratio?
quiz.a: Bending normal stress is larger. σ<sub>max</sub> = 32M/(πd³) and τ<sub>max</sub> = 16T/(πd³). With M = T, σ<sub>max</sub>/τ<sub>max</sub> = 2.

quiz.q: Why is J = 2I for a solid circular section?
quiz.a: For a circle, I = πd⁴/64 and J = πd⁴/32. The polar second moment includes resistance in two perpendicular directions about the axis, so J = I + I = 2I for a circular section.

quiz.q: State three assumptions of the bending formula σ = My/I.
quiz.a: Linear elastic material; small deflection; plane sections remain plane. The section is also away from local loads and supports.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these three formulas feed shaft sizing spreadsheets and finite element checks; FEA replaces P/A, My/I and Tr/J when the section is not simple or loads are local. Search for section modulus, polar moment of inertia and von Mises stress next. Newer curricula add combined loading and fatigue early, so Unit 2 follows naturally.
